Partially observable MDPs

In this chapter, we discuss POMDPs.

1What are POMDPs?discuss!¶

import stormpy
import sympy
import stormvogel as sv
import stormvogel.teaching as teach
import stormvogel.bird as bird
from stormvogel.to_dot import plot_model_pydot
sympy.init_printing()
from IPython.display import Math
from fractions import Fraction
Example 1

Consider the Monty-hall problem: You play in a game show, there are three doors, behind one of these doors is a car, behind the other doors are goats. The assumption here is that you want to win the car. You must pick a door, and without any information here, any pick is equally good. Now the game master interfers: They reveal that after a randomly picked door different then the one you picked is a goat. The game master now asks you whether you want to stick to your choice or change. The simple question is? Should you change. To answer this question, you may be tempted to construct the following MDP:

Source
from stormvogel.examples import create_condensed_monty_hall
monty_hall_mdp = create_condensed_monty_hall().copy().make_fully_observable()
plot_model_pydot(monty_hall_mdp)
Loading...

Let’s look at the optimal probability to win (and the policy that is optimal):

Source
result = sv.model_checking(monty_hall_mdp, 'Pmax=? [F "win"]')
print(f"Optimal win probability: {result.at_init()}")
# TODO: visualise scheduler
Optimal win probability: 1.0

The fully observable MDP admits a policy that wins with probability 1: stay at g′g'g′ (the initial pick was correct) and switch at b′b'b′ (the initial pick was wrong). This policy, however, relies on distinguishing states g′g'g′ and b′b'b′ — that is, knowing whether the initial door choice was correct. In the actual game, the player has no access to this information.

The problem in the example above is that the agent (the player in the game show) can make decisions based on unavailable information. This analysis is thus inadequate for any purposes where you want to prove that a sensor-based system can achieve a goal or that an attacker cannot steal sensitive information. To overcome these limitations, POMDPs have been introduced. They model explicitly that at every state, only limited information is available.

Example 2

In the POMDP, observations hide the car’s location. States d1d_1d1​, d2d_2d2​, d3d_3d3​ share observation pick?: the player knows they must pick a door but cannot see where the car is. States ggg and bbb share observation switch?: after picking, the player cannot tell whether they chose correctly. States g′g'g′ and b′b'b′ share observation show!: after the host reveals a goat, the player still cannot tell whether their original pick was right.

Observation-based policies can therefore only act on these three observation phases. At observation pick? the player chooses one of three doors; at observation show! they choose to stay or switch. This gives 3×2=63 \times 2 = 63×2=6 deterministic observation-based policies (and their randomised convex combinations).

Source
from stormvogel.examples import create_condensed_monty_hall
monty_hall_pomdp = create_condensed_monty_hall()
plot_model_pydot(monty_hall_pomdp)
Loading...
Definition 1 (Partially Observable MDP)

A partially observable MDP (POMDP) is a triple ⟨M,Z,obs⟩\langle \mdp, \Obs, \obsfun \rangle⟨M,Z,obs⟩, where M\mdpM is an MDP with states SSS, Z\ObsZ is a finite nonempty set of observations, and obs ⁣:S→Distr(Z)\obsfun\colon S \rightarrow \Distr{\Obs}obs:S→Distr(Z) is a state-based observation function.

Remark 1

Beyond state-based observations, the literature also uses transition-based observations where information is shared when taking a transition. We do not use such models here.

Assumption

From here on, assume deterministic observations with the shape obs ⁣:S→Z\obsfun\colon S \rightarrow \Obsobs:S→Z. Any stochastic observation function can be transformed into a determinsitic one using a polynomial blowup.

Given the assumption on deterministic observations, we write

Sz={s∈S∣obs(s)=z}S_z = \{ s \in S \mid \obsfun(s) = z \}Sz​={s∈S∣obs(s)=z}
Assumption

For all s,s′∈Szs, s' \in S_zs,s′∈Sz​, we assume Aen(s)=Aen(s′)\EnAct{s} = \EnAct{s'}Aen​(s)=Aen​(s′). We then write Aen(z)\EnAct{z}Aen​(z) for the common set of enabled actions at observation zzz.

Definition 2 (Observation trace)

Given any path

ξ=s0→a0s1→a1s2→a2…\xi = s_0 \xrightarrow{a_0} s_1 \xrightarrow{a_1} s_2 \xrightarrow{a_2} \dotsξ=s0​a0​​s1​a1​​s2​a2​​…

the observation trace is

obs(ξ)=obs(s0)→a0obs(s1)→a1obs(s2)→a2…\obstr{\xi} = \obsfun(s_0) \xrightarrow{a_0} \obsfun(s_1) \xrightarrow{a_1} \obsfun(s_2) \xrightarrow{a_2} \dotsobs(ξ)=obs(s0​)a0​​obs(s1​)a1​​obs(s2​)a2​​…
Definition 3 (Observation-based policies)

A policy π\piπ is observation-based, if for ξ,ξ′∈Paths\xi, \xi' \in \Pathsξ,ξ′∈Paths

obs(ξ)=obs(ξ′) implies π(ξ)=π(ξ′).\obstr{\xi} = \obstr{\xi'} \text{ implies } \pi(\xi) = \pi(\xi').obs(ξ)=obs(ξ′) implies π(ξ)=π(ξ′).

1.1Reachability probabilities in POMDPsdiscuss!¶

1.1.1Problem statementsdiscuss!¶

Assumptions

1.1.2Difficulty of the problemdiscuss!¶

Before we go into details, let us review the famous cheese-maze POMDP. Even in this simple POMDP, adding memory is important to act optimally.

Example 3 (Optimal observation-based policies require memory)
Source
from stormvogel.examples import create_cheese_maze
cheese_maze = create_cheese_maze()
plot_model_pydot(cheese_maze)
Loading...

Consider the cheese maze POMDP with three vertical corridors. The agent starts uniformly in one of the (upper) cells of the three corridors; not on the top row. All cells within the corridors share the same observation NS\mathit{NS}NS, so from the current observation alone the agent cannot tell which corridor it is in. The middle corridor leads to the cheese; the outer two lead to the dragon. It is possible to reach the cheese with probability one. An optimal strategy first moves upwards. Once it hits the top row, it has uniquely determined the agent’s position. It then moves to the correct corridor and descends. A memoryless policy must apply the same action in every corridor --- with observation NS\mathit{NS}NS. Then, the agent must never descend while there is positive probability of being in a dragon corridor. But a policy that never descends never reaches the cheese either. Thus, a memoryless policy cannot reach the cheese with probability one.

Sometimes, memoryless policies are sufficient, but randomization may then still be necessary:

Example 4 (Optimal memoryless policies require randomization)

Consider the cheese maze, and assume the agent starts in one of the two top-corner cells (observations ES\mathit{ES}ES or SW\mathit{SW}SW, which are distinguishable). Even though the starting position is known, reaching the middle corridor requires traversing EW\mathit{EW}EW cells on the top row, which are all indistinguishable. In a memoryless setting, the action taken in an EW\mathit{EW}EW cell must be the same no matter how the agent arrived there. A deterministic memoryless policy fixes a single direction—left or right—at every EW\mathit{EW}EW cell, so from one of the two starting corners the agent always moves away from the middle corridor and can never reach the cheese. A randomising policy, by contrast, can assign a small probability to descending at each NS\mathit{NS}NS cell and a high probability to continuing along the top row. This way, whenever the agent happens to be above the cheese corridor, there is a positive probability of descending correctly, so the cheese is reached with probability one eventually. No deterministic memoryless policy achieves this.

In general, we cannot give an upper bound on the amount of memory necessary.

Example 5 (Supremum not attained)

Consider a POMDP with states LlL_lLl​, LrL_rLr​, RlR_lRl​, RrR_rRr​, goal state ggg, and failure state fff. States LlL_lLl​ and RlR_lRl​ share observation lll; states LrL_rLr​ and RrR_rRr​ share observation rrr: the agent sees only the last signal, not whether the hidden type is LLL or RRR. The start state distributes uniformly over all four, so both hidden types are initially equally likely to be true. The three actions are listen\mathsf{listen}listen, guessL\mathsf{guessL}guessL, and guessR\mathsf{guessR}guessR. Under listen\mathsf{listen}listen, LLL-states transition to LlL_lLl​ with probability 910\tfrac{9}{10}109​ and LrL_rLr​ with probability 110\tfrac{1}{10}101​; RRR-states transition to RrR_rRr​ with probability 910\tfrac{9}{10}109​ and RlR_lRl​ with probability 110\tfrac{1}{10}101​ — so the signal is informative but noisy. Under guessL\mathsf{guessL}guessL, the agent moves to ggg from any LLL-state and to fff from any RRR-state; guessR\mathsf{guessR}guessR is symmetric.

Source
from stormvogel.examples import create_sup_not_attained_pomdp
sup_model = create_sup_not_attained_pomdp()
plot_model_pydot(sup_model)
Loading...

The supremum equals 1. For any nnn, the agent can apply listen\mathsf{listen}listen nnn times and then guess the majority signal seen. By the law of large numbers, the probability of guessing correctly approaches 1 as n→∞n \to \inftyn→∞, so sup⁡πPrπ(◊g)=1\sup_\pi \pr^\pi(\lozenge g) = 1supπ​Prπ(◊g)=1.

No policy attains it. Every finite observation history has positive probability under both hidden states: for any sequence o1…oko_1 \dots o_ko1​…ok​,

Pr(o1…ok∣L)>0andPr(o1…ok∣R)>0.\pr(o_1\dots o_k \mid L) > 0 \quad \text{and} \quad \pr(o_1\dots o_k \mid R) > 0.Pr(o1​…ok​∣L)>0andPr(o1​…ok​∣R)>0.

Therefore, whenever a policy guesses, there is positive probability of being in the wrong hidden state and reaching fff. Thus Prπ(◊g)<1\pr^\pi(\lozenge g) < 1Prπ(◊g)<1 for every policy π\piπ, and the supremum is not attained.

This example is key to proving the following general theorem.

Theorem 1 (Optimal policies do not need to exist)

For a POMDP M\mdpM and target TTT, the supremum

sup⁡π observation-basedPrMπ(◊T)\sup_{\pi\ \text{observation-based}} \pr^\pi_\mdp(\lozenge T)π observation-basedsup​PrMπ​(◊T)

need not be attained: there may be no observation-based policy π∗\pi^*π∗ achieving this value.

Indeed, the unbounded amount of memory is at the root of an undecidability statement.

Theorem 2 (Undecidable)

The standard verification and planning problems for POMDPs with reachability objectives are undecidable.

1.2Beliefsdiscuss!¶

Above, we have seen that optimal policies must rely on information from the history. However, it turns out that the precise history is not necessary for optimal decisions. Instead, the policy depends on the belief, i.e., a distribution that captures the likelihood of being in a particular state, given the history of observations seen and actions taken.

Example 6 (4-State POMDP — Running Example)

We use the following POMDP as a running example throughout this chapter. States s1s_1s1​ and s2s_2s2​ share observation zzz and are therefore indistinguishable to the agent. Three actions are available: aaa leads deterministically to the target from s1s_1s1​ and to the sink from s2s_2s2​; bbb mixes the hidden state; ccc gives a partial chance of reaching the target from either state.

Source
from stormvogel.examples import create_4state_reachability_pomdp_variantb
model = create_4state_reachability_pomdp_variantb()
obsstates = sorted(model.compute_states_per_observation()[model.get_observation("z")], key=lambda s: s.friendly_name)
s1 = obsstates[0]
s2 = obsstates[1]
plot_model_pydot(model)

1.2.1Belief updatesdiscuss!¶

Definition 4 (Belief update)

In a belief bbb, taking action aaa yields an updated belief as follows. Let

P(b,a,z′):=∑s∈Sobs(b)b(s)⋅∑s′∈Sz′δ(s,a,s′)P(b,a,z') := \sum_{s \in S_{\obsfun(b)}} b(s) \cdot \sum_{s' \in S_{z'}} \delta(s,a,s')P(b,a,z′):=s∈Sobs(b)​∑​b(s)⋅s′∈Sz′​∑​δ(s,a,s′)

denote the probability of observing z′∈Zz' \in \Obsz′∈Z upon taking action a∈Aa \in Aa∈A in belief bbb.

If P(b,a,z′)>0P(b,a,z') > 0P(b,a,z′)>0, the corresponding successor belief b′=⟦b∣a,z′⟧b' = \llbracket b \mid a, z' \rrbracketb′=[[b∣a,z′]] with obs(b′)=z′\obsfun(b') = z'obs(b′)=z′ is defined component-wise as

⟦b∣a,z′⟧(s′):=∑s∈Sobs(b)b(s)⋅δ(s,a,s′)P(b,a,z′)\llbracket b \mid a, z' \rrbracket(s') := \frac{\sum_{s \in S_{\obsfun(b)}} b(s) \cdot \delta(s,a,s')} {P(b,a,z')}[[b∣a,z′]](s′):=P(b,a,z′)∑s∈Sobs(b)​​b(s)⋅δ(s,a,s′)​

for all s′∈Sz′s' \in S_{z'}s′∈Sz′​. Otherwise, ⟦b∣a,z′⟧\llbracket b \mid a, z' \rrbracket[[b∣a,z′]] is undefined.

Definition 5 (Belief for a path)

Given a ξ=s0→a0s1→a1…\xi = s_0 \xrightarrow{a_0} s_1 \xrightarrow{a_1} \dotsξ=s0​a0​​s1​a1​​…, the belief bξ∈Distr(S)b_\xi \in \Distr{S}bξ​∈Distr(S) is defined inductively:

  • For a path of length zero ξ=s0\xi = s_0ξ=s0​: bξ(s)=[s=s0]b_\xi(s) = \indicator{s = s_0}bξ​(s)=[s=s0​].

  • For an extended path:

    bξ⋅a⋅s′=⟦bξ∣a,obs(s′)⟧b_{\xi \cdot a \cdot s'} = \llbracket b_\xi \mid a, \obsfun(s') \rrbracketbξ⋅a⋅s′​=[[bξ​∣a,obs(s′)]]

    .

Naturally, the belief for two paths with the same observation trace coincides.

Example 7 (Belief updates on the 4-state POMDP)

We compute belief updates on the running example (Example 6), starting from the uniform belief binit={s1↦12,s2↦12}\binit = \{s_1 \mapsto \tfrac{1}{2}, s_2 \mapsto \tfrac{1}{2}\}binit​={s1​↦21​,s2​↦21​}.

The belief weight on the LLL variants grows with each lll observation, but never reaches 1 — reflecting that the hidden state can never be determined with certainty.

1.2.2Belief-based policiesdiscuss!¶

Given this notion of belief and the mapping from an observation trace to a belief, we now introduce policies that make decisions solely based on the belief of a path/of a trace.

Definition 6 (Belief-based policies)

A policy π\piπ is belief-based if there exists π^ ⁣:Distr(S)→Distr(A)\hat\pi \colon \Distr{S} \rightarrow \Distr{A}π^:Distr(S)→Distr(A) such that

π(ξ)=π^(bξ)for all ξ∈Paths.\pi(\xi) = \hat\pi(b_\xi) \quad \text{for all } \xi \in \Paths.π(ξ)=π^(bξ​)for all ξ∈Paths.
Lemma 1 (Belief-based implies observation-based)

Every belief-based policy is observation-based.

By induction on the definition of bξb_\xibξ​, equal observation traces yield equal beliefs: obs(ξ)=obs(ξ′)\obstr{\xi} = \obstr{\xi'}obs(ξ)=obs(ξ′) implies bξ=bξ′b_\xi = b_{\xi'}bξ​=bξ′​. Thus any belief-based policy is observation-based.

The converse does not hold in general: an observation-based policy may use the full observation history in a way that distinguishes two paths with equal beliefs, e.g., by counting steps or recalling past actions.

Theorem 3 (Belief-based policies are sufficient (for reachability))

For any POMDP M\mdpM,

sup⁡π observation-basedPrMπ(◊T)=sup⁡π belief-basedPrMπ(◊T).\sup_{\pi\ \text{observation-based}} \pr^\pi_\mdp(\lozenge T) = \sup_{\pi\ \text{belief-based}} \pr^\pi_\mdp(\lozenge T).π observation-basedsup​PrMπ​(◊T)=π belief-basedsup​PrMπ​(◊T).

1.2.3The belief MDPdiscuss!¶

Since belief-based policies are sufficient and the belief captures everything about the history that is relevant for future decisions, we can replace hidden states entirely with belief distributions, reducing the POMDP to a standard (infinite-state) MDP.

Definition 7 (Belief MDP)

The belief MDP of POMDP M\mathcal{M}M is the (infinite-state) MDP

MB=(B,A,δB),\mathcal{M}^B = (\mathcal{B}, A, \delta^B),MB=(B,A,δB),

with transition function

δB(b,a,b′)=[ b′=⟦b∣a,z′⟧ ]⋅P(b,a,z′)\delta^B(b,a,b') = [\, b' = \llbracket b \mid a,z' \rrbracket \,] \cdot P(b,a,z')δB(b,a,b′)=[b′=[[b∣a,z′]]]⋅P(b,a,z′)

where z′=obs(b′)z' = \obsfun(b')z′=obs(b′).

For a given initial state sinit\sinitsinit​, the initial belief is

binit={sinit↦1}\binit = \{ \sinit \mapsto 1 \}binit​={sinit​↦1}

This belief MDP is naively continuous state, but for finite POMDPs, the reachable state space of a belief MDP is infinite but countable.

Lemma 2 (Belief MDP size and shape)

  • The (reachable fragment) of a belief MDP has a countable number of states.

  • If the POMDP is acyclic, the belief MDP is acyclic and finite.

The optimal reachability probability in a belief MDP coincides with the optimal reachability probability in the POMDP.

Theorem 4

For POMDP M\mdpM with target T⊆ST \subseteq ST⊆S, let TB={b∈B∣supp(b)⊆T}T^B = \{ b \in \mathcal{B} \mid \mathrm{supp}(b) \subseteq T \}TB={b∈B∣supp(b)⊆T}. Then

sup⁡π observation-basedPrMπ(◊T)=sup⁡π∈ΠmdPrMBπ(◊TB).\sup_{\pi\ \text{observation-based}} \pr^\pi_\mdp(\lozenge T) = \sup_{\pi \in \MdPolicies} \pr^\pi_{\mathcal{M}^B}(\lozenge T^B).π observation-basedsup​PrMπ​(◊T)=π∈Πmd​sup​PrMBπ​(◊TB).

In particular, it suffices to consider deterministic belief-based policies!

1.2.4Belief-value functionsdiscuss!¶

For the belief MDP, we can consider the standard value function that maps a state of that MDP to a value of interest, in this case the maximal reachability probability. This function thus maps POMDP beliefs to probabilities, V ⁣:B→[0,1]V\colon \mathcal{B} \rightarrow [0,1]V:B→[0,1]. This function is of interest independent of the belief MDP.

Two structural properties are particularly relevant. First, under any fixed observation-based policy the belief-value function is affine in the belief.

Lemma 3

For any observation-based policy π\piπ, Vπ(b)=απ⋅bV^\pi(b) = \alpha^\pi \cdot bVπ(b)=απ⋅b for some vector απ∈[0,1]S\alpha^\pi \in [0,1]^Sαπ∈[0,1]S.

For a fixed observation-based policy π\piπ, the action taken at each step is determined by the observation-action history alone. The probability of any state trajectory ξ=s0→a0s1→a1⋯\xi = s_0 \xrightarrow{a_0} s_1 \xrightarrow{a_1} \cdotsξ=s0​a0​​s1​a1​​⋯ under π\piπ is therefore b(s0)⋅∏tδ(st,at,st+1)b(s_0) \cdot \prod_t \delta(s_t, a_t, s_{t+1})b(s0​)⋅∏t​δ(st​,at​,st+1​), which is linear in b(s0)b(s_0)b(s0​). Summing over all target-reaching trajectories gives

Vπ(b)=∑s∈Sb(s)⋅Prπ(◊T∣s0=s)⏟απ(s)=απ⋅b.V^\pi(b) = \sum_{s \in S} b(s) \cdot \underbrace{\pr^\pi(\lozenge T \mid s_0 = s)}_{\alpha^\pi(s)} = \alpha^\pi \cdot b.Vπ(b)=s∈S∑​b(s)⋅απ(s)Prπ(◊T∣s0​=s)​​=απ⋅b.
Example 8 (Alpha vectors on the 4-state POMDP)

Consider the two single-step memoryless policies on Example 6: always take action aaa, or always take action ccc. For policy πa\pi_aπa​: from s1s_1s1​ action aaa reaches the target with probability 1; from s2s_2s2​ with probability 0. For policy πc\pi_cπc​: from s1s_1s1​ action ccc reaches the target with probability 14\tfrac{1}{4}41​; from s2s_2s2​ with probability 45\tfrac{4}{5}54​. The two alpha vectors are therefore απa=(1, 0)\alpha^{\pi_a} = (1,\, 0)απa​=(1,0) and απc=(14, 45)\alpha^{\pi_c} = (\tfrac{1}{4},\, \tfrac{4}{5})απc​=(41​,54​), and the value functions

Vπa(b)=b(s1),Vπc(b)=14 b(s1)+45 b(s2)V^{\pi_a}(b) = b(s_1), \qquad V^{\pi_c}(b) = \tfrac{1}{4}\,b(s_1) + \tfrac{4}{5}\,b(s_2)Vπa​(b)=b(s1​),Vπc​(b)=41​b(s1​)+54​b(s2​)

are both linear in bbb.

Source

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

b1_range = np.linspace(0, 1, 200)
v_a = b1_range
v_c = (1/4) * b1_range + (4/5) * (1 - b1_range)

plt.plot(b1_range, v_a, label=r"$V^{\pi_a}(b)$")
plt.plot(b1_range, v_c, label=r"$V^{\pi_c}(b)$")

Such an affine function is called an alpha vector:

Definition 8 (Alpha vector)

An alpha vector is a function α ⁣:S→[0,1]\alpha \colon S \rightarrow [0,1]α:S→[0,1]. For a belief b∈Bb \in \mathcal{B}b∈B, the value under α\alphaα is the dot product, i.e.,

α⋅b=∑s∈Sα(s)⋅b(s).\alpha \cdot b = \sum_{s \in S} \alpha(s) \cdot b(s).α⋅b=s∈S∑​α(s)⋅b(s).
Lemma 4

The belief-value function for a fixed observation-based policy π\piπ is an alpha-vector.

Second, the optimal belief-value function is the pointwise supremum over alpha vectors:

V∗(b)=sup⁡α∈Γ  α⋅b,V^*(b) = \sup_{\alpha \in \Gamma} \; \alpha \cdot b,V∗(b)=α∈Γsup​α⋅b,

where Γ\GammaΓ is the set of alpha vectors representing all relevant (in general, belief-based deterministic) policies.

Lemma 5

V∗(b)V^*(b)V∗(b) is convex.

Note that if it suffices to only consider a finite set of such policies, V∗(b)V^*(b)V∗(b) is piecewise linear.

2Algorithms for POMDPsdiscuss!¶

Since exact computation is undecidable (Theorem 2) and an optimal policy need not exist (Theorem 1), in practice one computes bounds on the optimal value V∗(binit)V^*(\binit)V∗(binit​). We construct a number of different algorithms, for either computing lower bounds (mostly for planning) or upper bounds (mostly for verification) of the maximal reachability probability. The ideas can be lifted to minimal reachability probabilities and to expected reachability rewards and discounted total rewards as usual. Supporting richer temporal properties is a bit more involved.

We split the algorithmic ideas into

  1. operating directly on a finite MDP abstraction,

  2. operating over weaker policy classes,

  3. operating over stronger policy classes, and

  4. operating symbolically in belief space.

2.1Algorithms based on finite MDPsdiscuss!¶

The main idea for these algorithms is simple: We construct a finite MDP that relates to the POMDP and use standard techniques. In particular, we typically construct a finite MDP that abstracts the infinite belief MDP.

2.1.1Finite belief MDP unfoldingdiscuss!¶

From a verification perspective, operating immediately on the belief MDP is very convenient. As this MDP is infinite in general, we may explore a finite fragment of this MDP. The finite belief MDP unfolding explores MB\mathcal{M}^BMB from the initial belief binit\binitbinit​, expanding at most KKK distinct belief states. Any successor belief that falls outside the budget is called a frontier belief. To make the finite fragment a proper MDP, we can add transitions from the frontier belief states to either a target or sink state. The way we handle these frontier beliefs is generally controlled by a cutoff function c ⁣:S→[0,1]c\colon S \rightarrow [0,1]c:S→[0,1].

Definition 9 (Finite belief MDP)

Fix a POMDP M\mathcal{M}M, a budget K∈NK \in \mathbb{N}K∈N, and a cutoff function c ⁣:S→[0,1]c\colon S \to [0,1]c:S→[0,1]. Let BK⊆B\mathcal{B}^K \subseteq \mathcal{B}BK⊆B be the set of at most KKK distinct beliefs discovered by BFS from binit\binitbinit​. The finite belief MDP MB,K,c\mathcal{M}^{B,K,c}MB,K,c agrees with MB\mathcal{M}^BMB on all beliefs in BK\mathcal{B}^KBK, and associates with each frontier belief bf∉BKb_f \notin \mathcal{B}^Kbf​∈/BK a single absorbing “cut” action:

δB,K,c(bf,cut,TB)=c⋅bf,δB,K,c(bf,cut,⊥)=1−c⋅bf,\delta^{B,K,c}(b_f, \mathrm{cut}, T^B) = c \cdot b_f, \qquad \delta^{B,K,c}(b_f, \mathrm{cut}, \bot) = 1 - c \cdot b_f,δB,K,c(bf​,cut,TB)=c⋅bf​,δB,K,c(bf​,cut,⊥)=1−c⋅bf​,

where c⋅bf=∑s∈Sc(s) bf(s)c \cdot b_f = \sum_{s \in S} c(s)\, b_f(s)c⋅bf​=∑s∈S​c(s)bf​(s) and ⊥\bot⊥ is a fresh absorbing sink state.

Theorem 5 (Over- and under-approximation)

Let V∗V^*V∗ be the optimal reachability probability in MB\mathcal{M}^BMB, and VK,cV^{K,c}VK,c the optimal reachability probability in MB,K,c\mathcal{M}^{B,K,c}MB,K,c.

  • If c(s)≥V∗(s)c(s) \geq V^*(s)c(s)≥V∗(s) for all s∈Ss \in Ss∈S: VK,c(binit)≥V∗(binit)V^{K,c}(\binit) \geq V^*(\binit)VK,c(binit​)≥V∗(binit​) (over-approximation).

  • If for some policy π\piπ, c(s)≤Vπ(s)c(s) \leq V^\pi(s)c(s)≤Vπ(s) for all s∈Ss \in Ss∈S: VK,c(binit)≤V∗(binit)V^{K,c}(\binit) \leq V^*(\binit)VK,c(binit​)≤V∗(binit​) (under-approximation).

In particular, c≡1c \equiv 1c≡1 is always optimistic and c≡0c \equiv 0c≡0 is always pessimistic. As K→∞K \to \inftyK→∞, both bounds converge to V∗(binit)V^*(\binit)V∗(binit​).

We note the asymetry: Upper bounds are correct using the convexity, whereas the lower bounds must consistently under-approximate a single policy (to then also be affine and thus convex).

Note that computing such cut-offs is simple:

  • For lower bounds, picking π\piπ and evaluating any (e.g., memoryless) observation-based policy yields a pessimistic bound.

  • For upper bounds, assuming the POMDP is fully observable yields an optimistic bound.

However, the computational challenge is to find good cut-off policies with limited overhead. We discuss some strategies to do so Section 2.2 and Section 2.3, respectively.

Example 9

We construct the finite belief MDP for the 4-state POMDP with initial belief binit={s1↦12, s2↦12}\binit = \{s_1 \mapsto \tfrac{1}{2},\, s_2 \mapsto \tfrac{1}{2}\}binit​={s1​↦21​,s2​↦21​}.

Source
from fractions import Fraction
from stormvogel.teaching.belief_mdp import belief_mdp

initial_belief = {s1: Fraction(1, 2), s2: Fraction(1, 2)}
bmdp_lower = belief_mdp(model, initial_belief, cutoff=0, max_states=5)
bmdp_upper = belief_mdp(model, initial_belief, cutoff=1, max_states=5)
plot_model_pydot(bmdp_lower)
plot_model_pydot(bmdp_upper)
Loading...

With a restricted budget, frontier beliefs appear. The pessimistic (c=0c = 0c=0) and optimistic (c=1c = 1c=1) unfoldings give lower and upper bounds on V∗V^*V∗:

Source
result_lower = sv.model_checking(bmdp_lower, 'Pmax=? [F "target"]')
result_upper = sv.model_checking(bmdp_upper, 'Pmax=? [F "target"]')
print(f"Lower bound: {result_lower.at_init()}")
print(f"Upper bound: {result_upper.at_init()}")
Lower bound: 0.7256944444444444
Upper bound: 1.0

The finite exploration above is general, but practically only works well if the (reachable fragment of the) belief MDP is small or in presence of good cut-off values.

2.1.2Lovejoy grid discretisationdiscuss!¶

In a verification context, proving that no policy achieves a target with a probability above a threshold is arguably the most important task. We note that finite belief MDP unrollings tend to converge slowly to useful upper bounds. On typical problem is that every step in a belief MDP may only change the belief a tiny bit, so belief MDPs quickly grow out of reasonable bounds. The following complementary approach constructs a finite MDP that yields overapproximations without relying on cut-off values. The key idea is to ensure finite exploration by fixing a finite grid (a point set) B^⊂B\hat{\mathcal{B}} \subset \mathcal{B}B^⊂B upfront. Any belief b′∉B^b' \notin \hat{\mathcal{B}}b′∈/B^ that arises as a successor is not added directly to the state space; instead the belief is represented as a convex combination of the nearest grid points.

The value of such a belief that is not in the point set can be approximated from above by using the convexity of the value function.

Definition 10 (Convex grid interpolation)

Let B^={b^1,…,b^m}\hat{\mathcal{B}} = \{\hat{b}_1, \dots, \hat{b}_m\}B^={b^1​,…,b^m​} be a finite set of beliefs whose convex hull covers B\mathcal{B}B. For any belief b′∈Bb' \in \mathcal{B}b′∈B, write b′=∑i=1mλib^ib' = \sum_{i=1}^m \lambda_i \hat{b}_ib′=∑i=1m​λi​b^i​ with λi≥0\lambda_i \geq 0λi​≥0, ∑iλi=1\sum_i \lambda_i = 1∑i​λi​=1. The grid-interpolated value is

V^(b′)=∑i=1mλiV^(b^i).\hat{V}(b') = \sum_{i=1}^m \lambda_i \hat{V}(\hat{b}_i).V^(b′)=i=1∑m​λi​V^(b^i​).

Because V∗V^*V∗ is convex, the interpolated value is an over-approximation:

V∗(b′)=V∗ ⁣(∑iλib^i)≤∑iλiV∗(b^i)≤V^(b′).V^*(b') = V^*\!\left(\sum_i \lambda_i \hat{b}_i\right) \leq \sum_i \lambda_i V^*(\hat{b}_i) \leq \hat{V}(b').V∗(b′)=V∗(i∑​λi​b^i​)≤i∑​λi​V∗(b^i​)≤V^(b′).

This value-level observation motivates a concrete finite MDP construction: rather than storing off-grid beliefs as states, redirect every transition that would land on b′∉B^b' \notin \hat{\mathcal{B}}b′∈/B^ to a distribution over grid beliefs, using the same convex weights λi\lambda_iλi​.

Definition 11 (Lovejoy grid MDP)

Let B^\hat{\mathcal{B}}B^ be a finite grid whose convex hull covers B\mathcal{B}B. For each b′∈Bb' \in \mathcal{B}b′∈B, fix convex weights λ(b′,b^′)≥0\lambda(b', \hat{b}') \geq 0λ(b′,b^′)≥0 with ∑b^′∈B^λ(b′,b^′)=1\sum_{\hat{b}' \in \hat{\mathcal{B}}} \lambda(b', \hat{b}') = 1∑b^′∈B^​λ(b′,b^′)=1 such that b′=∑b^′∈B^λ(b′,b^′) b^′b' = \sum_{\hat{b}' \in \hat{\mathcal{B}}} \lambda(b', \hat{b}')\, \hat{b}'b′=∑b^′∈B^​λ(b′,b^′)b^′, where λ(b^′,b^′)=1\lambda(\hat{b}', \hat{b}') = 1λ(b^′,b^′)=1 for on-grid beliefs. The Lovejoy grid MDP M^\hat{\mdp}M^ has state space B^\hat{\mathcal{B}}B^ and transition function

δ^(b^,a,b^′)=∑b′∈BδB(b^,a,b′)⋅λ(b′,b^′).\hat{\delta}(\hat{b}, a, \hat{b}') = \sum_{b' \in \mathcal{B}} \delta^B(\hat{b}, a, b') \cdot \lambda(b', \hat{b}').δ^(b^,a,b^′)=b′∈B∑​δB(b^,a,b′)⋅λ(b′,b^′).
Theorem 6

The maximal reachability probability in M^\hat{\mdp}M^ is an upper bound on V∗(binit)V^*(\binit)V∗(binit​).

We remark that building the convex weights is not always trivial. However, when there are only two states per observation, computing these weights becomes reasonably straightforward using linear interpolation.

Example 10

We apply the Lovejoy construction to the 4-state POMDP (Example 6) with initial belief binit={s1↦12,s2↦12}\binit = \{s_1 \mapsto \tfrac{1}{2}, s_2 \mapsto \tfrac{1}{2}\}binit​={s1​↦21​,s2​↦21​} and grid resolution k=8k = 8k=8.

Source
from stormvogel.teaching.lovejoy import lovejoy_grid_mdp

lovejoy_mdp = lovejoy_grid_mdp(model, {s1: Fraction(1, 2), s2: Fraction(1, 2)}, k=8)
plot_model_pydot(lovejoy_mdp)
result = sv.model_checking(lovejoy_mdp, 'Pmax=? [F "target"]')
print(f"Lovejoy upper bound: {result.at_init()}")
Loading...

Increasing kkk refines the grid and tightens the upper bound.

Example 11

We apply the Lovejoy construction to the supremum-not-attained POMDP (Example 5). Note that the upper bound here is trivially one (as it is also the supremum). However, the example nicely shows the approximation. We take the initial belief binit={Ll↦12,Rl↦12}\binit = \{L_l \mapsto \tfrac{1}{2}, R_l \mapsto \tfrac{1}{2}\}binit​={Ll​↦21​,Rl​↦21​} and grid resolution k=8k = 8k=8.

2.2Lower bounds from memoryless policiesdiscuss!¶

The optimal policy for a POMDP may in general require unbounded memory. A natural restriction is to memoryless policies, which choose an action based only on the current observation. We have seen that for some POMDPs, memoryless policies are actually sufficient.

Definition 12 (Memoryless observation-based policy)

An observation-based memoryless policy π\piπ is a function π ⁣:Z→Distr(A)\pi\colon \Obs \to \Distr{A}π:Z→Distr(A).

Since every memoryless policy is a special case of an observation-based policy:

sup⁡σ memorylessPrMσ(◊T)  ≤  V∗(binit).\sup_{\sigma\ \text{memoryless}} \pr^\sigma_\mdp(\lozenge T) \;\leq\; V^*(\binit).σ memorylesssup​PrMσ​(◊T)≤V∗(binit​).

Optimising over memoryless policies therefore yields a lower bound on the optimal value. Memoryless policies also often yield helpful bounds for finite belief MDP constructions.

2.2.1Reduction to a parametric Markov chaindiscuss!¶

A memoryless policy is fully determined by action probabilities yz,a∈[0,1]y_{z,a} \in [0,1]yz,a​∈[0,1] for each observation z∈Zz \in \Obsz∈Z and action a∈Aen(z)a \in \EnAct{z}a∈Aen​(z), subject to ∑ayz,a=1\sum_{a} y_{z,a} = 1∑a​yz,a​=1. Because the policy is observation-based, all states s∈Szs \in S_zs∈Sz​ sharing observation zzz must use the same distribution, so they share the same parameters. This leads naturally to a parametric Markov chain (pMC), extending the corresponding pMC for MDPs to the POMDP setting by grouping parameters by observation class.

Definition 13 (Corresponding pMC for POMDP)

Extending the corresponding pMC for MDPs, the corresponding pMC DMD_\mdpDM​ for POMDP M\mdpM has the same state space and introduces parameters y={yz,a∣z∈Z, a∈Aen(z)}\mathbf{y} = \{y_{z,a} \mid z \in \Obs,\, a \in \EnAct{z}\}y={yz,a​∣z∈Z,a∈Aen​(z)}, shared across all states with the same observation. The transition function is

δD(s,s′)={δ(s,a,s′)if Aen(obs(s))={a},∑a∈Aen(obs(s))yobs(s), a⋅δ(s,a,s′)otherwise.\delta_{D}(s, s') = \begin{cases} \delta(s, a, s') & \text{if } \EnAct{\obsfun(s)} = \{a\}, \\[4pt] \displaystyle\sum_{a \in \EnAct{\obsfun(s)}} y_{\obsfun(s),\,a} \cdot \delta(s, a, s') & \text{otherwise.} \end{cases}δD​(s,s′)=⎩⎨⎧​δ(s,a,s′)a∈Aen​(obs(s))∑​yobs(s),a​⋅δ(s,a,s′)​if Aen​(obs(s))={a},otherwise.​
Example 12

Applying the transformation to the 4-state POMDP: states s1s_1s1​ and s2s_2s2​ share observation zzz, so they get the same policy parameters.

Source
from stormvogel.teaching.policy_to_pmc import policy_to_pmc

pmc = policy_to_pmc(model)
plot_model_pydot(pmc)
Loading...

Every memoryless policy π\piπ corresponds to a well-defined valuation val\valval of y\mathbf{y}y, and vice versa: the induced Markov chain M[π]\mdp[\pi]M[π] equals the instantiated pMC DM[val]D_\mdp[\val]DM​[val]. The reachability probability f(val)=PrMσ(◊T)f(\val) = \pr^\sigma_\mdp(\lozenge T)f(val)=PrMσ​(◊T) is therefore a rational function of y\mathbf{y}y, as studied in the parametric chapter.

Theorem 7
sup⁡σ memorylessPrMσ(◊T)  =  max⁡val well-defined for DMf(val).\sup_{\sigma\ \text{memoryless}} \pr^\sigma_\mdp(\lozenge T) \;=\; \max_{\val\ \text{well-defined for}\ D_\mdp} f(\val).σ memorylesssup​PrMσ​(◊T)=val well-defined for DM​max​f(val).

This reduces finding the best memoryless policy to parameter synthesis for pMCs: maximising the rational function fff over the policy simplex. The number of parameters is O(∣Z∣⋅max⁡z∣Aen(z)∣)O(|\Obs| \cdot \max_z |\EnAct{z}|)O(∣Z∣⋅maxz​∣Aen​(z)∣).

2.2.2Adding memorydiscuss!¶

Similar to goal unfoldings, specific memorystructures can be folded into the POMDP. Asking for a memoryless policy on this larger POMDP is then equivalent to asking for a finite state controller in a smaller POMDP. While the POMDP grows only polynomially in the number of memory states added, a polynomial growth in the number of parameters makes this quickly infeasible.

2.2.3Hardness of the problemdiscuss!¶

The existence of a memoryless policy satisfying a reachability threshold is indeed ETR-complete, via the polynomial-time equivalence between this problem and feasibility synthesis for pMCs. Note that these notes do not show the direction from parametric models to POMDPs.

2.3Upper bounds from revealing informationdiscuss!¶

A natural upper bound on the belief value function V∗(b)V^*(b)V∗(b) is obtained by giving the policies more information, i.e., by optimising over a larger set of policies. Optimising over larger sets of policies can be simpler: The simplest larger class of policies to consider are MDP policies that fully observe the current state. The optimal value in for those policies (i.e., the optimal value in the underlying MDP) is a natural upper bound on the optimal value under observation-based policies. We consider this upper bound and a tighter variation thereof.

2.3.1MDP upper bounddiscuss!¶

Lifting the fully observable MDP value function VMDPV_\mathrm{MDP}VMDP​ to beliefs by expectation gives

VMDP(b)=∑s∈Sb(s) VMDP(s).V_\mathrm{MDP}(b) = \sum_{s \in S} b(s)\, V_\mathrm{MDP}(s).VMDP​(b)=s∈S∑​b(s)VMDP​(s).

This is optimistic: different states in the belief support can implicitly choose different optimal actions, as if the agent knew the hidden state exactly.

2.3.2QMDPdiscuss!¶

The QMDP approximation requires a single action to be chosen under the current belief, but then assumes the state becomes fully observable for all future decisions:

VQMDP(b)=max⁡a∈A∑s∈Sb(s)∑s′∈Sδ(s,a,s′) VMDP(s′).V_\mathrm{QMDP}(b) = \max_{a \in A} \sum_{s \in S} b(s) \sum_{s' \in S} \delta(s,a,s')\, V_\mathrm{MDP}(s').VQMDP​(b)=a∈Amax​s∈S∑​b(s)s′∈S∑​δ(s,a,s′)VMDP​(s′).
Theorem 8

For every belief b∈Bb \in \mathcal{B}b∈B,

V∗(b)  ≤  VQMDP(b)  ≤  VMDP(b).V^*(b) \;\leq\; V_\mathrm{QMDP}(b) \;\leq\; V_\mathrm{MDP}(b).V∗(b)≤VQMDP​(b)≤VMDP​(b).

QMDP is therefore always a tighter upper bound than the plain MDP value.

Example 13
Source
from stormvogel.examples import create_two_state_commitment_pomdp
from stormvogel.teaching.pomdp_backup import (
    AlphaVI, initial_alpha, make_operator_pomdp_maxreachprob_exact,
    mdp_bound_alpha, qmdp_alphas, plot_value_function_comparison,
)

model = create_two_state_commitment_pomdp()
plot_model_pydot(model)
obsstates = sorted(model.compute_states_per_observation()[model.get_observation("z")], key=lambda s: s.friendly_name)
s1, s2 = obsstates[0], obsstates[1]

op = make_operator_pomdp_maxreachprob_exact(model, "target")
vi = AlphaVI(op, [initial_alpha(model, "target")])
for _ in range(5):
    vi.step()

ax = plot_value_function_comparison(
    [
        (vi.current_alphas,               "exact VI (k=5)"),
        (qmdp_alphas(model, "target"),    "QMDP"),
        ([mdp_bound_alpha(model, "target")], "MDP bound"),
    ],
    s1, s2,

2.3.3Fast Informed Bounds and Tighter Informed Boundsdiscuss!¶

The idea of VQMDPV_\mathrm{QMDP}VQMDP​ can be taken further. QMDP assumes full observability after a single action; one can instead delay that assumption for k≥1k \geq 1k≥1 steps. The agent optimises over the next kkk actions under partial observability — taking into account the observations received — and then falls back to the fully-observable MDP value. Increasing kkk yields tighter upper bounds at the cost of an optimisation that is exponential in kkk. Fast informed bounds (FIB) Hauskrecht (2000) and tighter informed bounds (TIB) Krale et al. (2025) are two concrete instantiations of this idea that differ in how the kkk-step optimisation is carried out.

2.4Value iteration in belief spacediscuss!¶

The Bellman operator lifts naturally to beliefs:

Definition 14 (Belief-space Bellman operator)

The belief-space Bellman operator Φ\PhiΦ acts on V ⁣:B→[0,1]V \colon \mathcal{B} \rightarrow [0,1]V:B→[0,1] by

(ΦV)(b)={1if b∈TB,max⁡a∈A∑z′∈ZP(b,a,z′)⋅V ⁣(⟦b∣a,z′⟧)otherwise.(\Phi V)(b) = \begin{cases} 1 & \text{if } b \in T^B, \\ \displaystyle\max_{a \in A} \sum_{z' \in \Obs} P(b,a,z') \cdot V\!\left(\llbracket b \mid a, z' \rrbracket\right) & \text{otherwise.}\end{cases}(ΦV)(b)=⎩⎨⎧​1a∈Amax​z′∈Z∑​P(b,a,z′)⋅V([[b∣a,z′]])​if b∈TB,otherwise.​

Initialised with the target indicator V0(b)=[supp(b)⊆T]V_0(b) = \indicator{\mathrm{supp}(b) \subseteq T}V0​(b)=[supp(b)⊆T], one application yields the one-step reachability probability, and iterating converges to V∗V^*V∗.
